label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
# Cup Day, One Dead Coolroom and Fourteen Bags of Ice

Jonno,

You keep asking what happened to the coolroom during Cup week, so here it is. Consider this your official briefing. I’m not typing it out again in messages with my thumbs like some sort of Victorian peasant.

Also, London has made you soft, so try not to get distressed halfway through. You’d have cried.

The compressor carked it sometime between Monday night and Tuesday morning. I found out at 6.40am on Cup Day when I opened the coolroom and got hit by air that was, at best, personally disappointing. Thermometer said 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Not ideal, generally speaking, when you’ve got 140 covers booked for lunch, a three-course set menu and a coolroom full of things that need to be cold.

I stood there looking at the thermometer for a bit, like eye contact was going to restart the compressor. Gave the unit a little knock too, because apparently I’m an electrician when I’m desperate. Nothing. Dead as.

Raff was away, so it was me running it. Excellent. Exactly how I like to start a public holiday: alone with my thoughts and several hundred kilos of increasingly optimistic stock.

I rang Wally from Coldline. Wally couldn’t come until Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney.

Wednesday.

The day after Cup Day.

Perfect. No notes. Perhaps Sydney could also send us a fridge while it was at it.

Phil’s contribution was: “Just make it work, mate.”

Which, as you know, is not a plan. It’s barely even a sentence. No one in the history of commercial kitchens has heard “just make it work” and suddenly discovered a spare compressor in their apron. Cheers, Phil. I was going to deliberately ruin lunch, but now you’ve refocused me.

So we started moving everything.

We squeezed whatever we could into the two undercounters and the bar fridge. You’ve never truly understood your own kitchen until you’re squatting in front of an undercounter at 7am trying to work out whether six trays of beef can occupy the same physical space as a stack of containers and your remaining patience.

The bar fridge stopped looking like a fridge and started looking like a game of Tetris designed by someone who hates you.

Then Marta from the cafe next door, actual saint, let us use half her walk-in. She didn’t make a big thing of it, just told us to bring it through. This is why you stay nice to your neighbours, Jonno. Not because it’s morally correct. Because one day your coolroom will die and you’ll need somewhere to put 30 kilos of beef shin.

Marta’s kindness did come at a price, obviously. We had to pay her back in croissant credit. I think I owe her about three weeks of staff meal at this point. Every time she looks at me now I can see her calculating pastry. Fair enough. Half her walk-in was full of my problems.

The stock run to Marta’s was also when the morning really found its rhythm.

Me and Benny loaded 30kg of beef shin onto the milk crate trolley and headed down the laneway. In the rain. Because of course it was raining. About halfway down, one of the wheels fell off.

Not loosened. Fell off.

So there we were: two fully grown hospitality professionals, 30kg of shin, a trolley with three wheels and absolutely no dignity left. Benny did that thing where you start laughing but you’re also trying not to drop expensive meat, so it comes out as this weird wheezing noise. I told him to pull himself together. Then the trolley lurched again and I nearly sat down in a puddle.

You’d have been useless. You’d have stood there saying, “This is actually insane,” instead of lifting anything. I know this because it’s what you used to do when the grill was busy.

Meanwhile, Kev, our dishy and the only person who seemed to be enjoying himself, went to the servo for ice. He came back with fourteen bags and filled the old esky.

The bloke at the servo asked if we were having a party.

Yeah, mate. Huge party. Very exclusive. It’s called Refrigeration Failure and everyone’s invited except the duck legs.

I lost about $1,800 worth of stock all up, mostly dairy and the duck legs. And before my mum reads this and rings me: yes, we threw out what needed throwing out. No, we did not give the duck legs “a bit of a smell” and send them anyway.

Still hurt though. Eighteen hundred bucks into the bin before the first booking had even sat down. You don’t need to make a dramatic speech about it. You just stand there for a second, look at the bin, then keep going because it’s 9am and you’ve still got lunch to cook.

By service, we had a system. A shit system, granted, but a system.

Undercounters rammed. Bar fridge rammed. Marta’s walk-in half ours. Kev’s esky full of servo ice. Everyone knew where things were as long as nobody moved anything, opened the wrong door or asked a complicated question.

And here’s the idiotic part: service was unbelievable.

Not “unbelievable” in the sense that everything went smoothly. Obviously it didn’t. I mean everyone was locked in. No wandering off. No standing around discussing whose section was worse. No ten-minute philosophical debate about the pass. Just tickets coming in and food going out.

There’s something beautiful about a kitchen when everyone stops performing being busy and actually gets busy. You would’ve hated how much you loved it.

Then at 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

Now, you remember the panna cotta. People would order it after claiming they were “too full for dessert”, which is always a lie. We’d set them, turn them out, everyone’s happy, small victory for dairy.

Not this time.

So dessert became **affogato with whatever**.

That was genuinely the name we were using. Not on the printed menu, obviously. We hadn’t completely lost our minds. But that’s what it was: affogato, plus whatever we had that could reasonably join it on the plate without anyone calling Fair Trading.

And people loved it.

Loved it more than the panna cotta.

We had tables acting like we’d invented coffee and ice cream that afternoon. One bloke told Benny it was “a really clever finish”. Mate, it was a fridge accident with a biscuit.

There’s no justice in cooking.

Best table of the day was table 9. A woman there had watched some of our laneway operation through the window. When her main came out, she asked whether the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

I hope she’s doing well. I hope she wins money she doesn’t need and finds a parking spot directly outside every destination for the rest of her life.

We even had a horse in the sweep to keep morale up. Mine was called Ice Cold Lad.

Ice Cold Lad.

On the day the coolroom died.

He came second last.

Not even last, which would at least have shown some commitment. Second last. Just trotted around out the back like he’d also been told the part wasn’t arriving until Wednesday.

At that point you’ve got to accept the universe is taking the piss.

The funny thing is, by the end of lunch, nobody wanted to say it was a disaster because it honestly didn’t feel like one. It felt like the best service we’d done all year. Everyone was stuffed, wet in Benny’s and my case, and probably owed Marta several laminated pastries, but we’d fed 140 people and done a proper job under genuinely stupid circumstances.

That’s the bit people don’t get unless they’ve worked in a place like ours. The coolroom dying wasn’t the whole story. The whole story was Kev coming back with fourteen bags of ice. Marta clearing half her walk-in. Benny laughing so hard at a broken trolley that he nearly dropped the beef. Everybody just getting on with it without waiting for someone to deliver a rousing speech beside the rice cooker.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite.

Anyway, that’s what happened. You’d have absolutely lost your mind. You’d have made three panicked lists, complained about the rain, then tried to reorganise the bar fridge while everyone was still using it. London might’ve taken your tolerance for filthy weather, but I’m confident your ability to panic without contributing remains intact.

I’ll expect your response promptly. And yes, I know you’ll just send back “hahahaha fuck that” instead of appreciating the effort involved.

Come home, ya flog.
